headline: World court: Myanmar committed genocide.
summary: The UN's top court ruled 9-6 Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017. The judges found Myanmar's forces killed about 10,000 people; more than 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. No state had been found guilty of genocide before. The court ordered reparations and a right of return. It cannot enforce either.

cover_question.q: What if Myanmar just ignores it?

cover_answer: The world now has a ruling to hold up. That's something.
table_question: A referee calls a foul but can't enforce it. Does the call count?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In a country far away called Myanmar, soldiers hurt a group of people called the Rohingya, and most of them had to run to the next country. Today the world's top judges said out loud that it was wrong. The Rohingya families cried and hugged when they heard. You are safe, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Someone said it was wrong, out loud. That's the one piece they can hold.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script picks it: judges saying out loud that it was wrong, and families hugging with relief. Cantor found this age fears 'could it happen to me?', so 'far away' and 'you are safe' get said. Expect 'did the bad guys go to jail?' No. The judges have no jail.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 2017 Myanmar's army attacked the Rohingya, a Muslim minority. About 10,000 were killed and 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. The world's top court weighed the evidence and ruled 9 to 6: genocide, a first for any country. It can't make arrests. It can tell the world.
8-12.why: A referee who sees everything and enforces nothing.
8-12.why_long: At twelve a child tests whether rules get applied, and this one gives them a referee who made a call he cannot enforce. The script runs the chain: attack, evidence, a 9 to 6 vote, then the gap. Expect 'what happens now?' Myanmar must let the refugees home and pay. Whether it does is up to the countries that lean on it.

13-17.script: The court ruled 9-6. Six judges of fifteen saw the same evidence and did not call it genocide. Does the split weaken the ruling, or is that what a real court looks like? Second: Britain expelled Myanmar's defense attache the same day. Enforcement, or a gesture?
13-17.why: Two things to hold: a historic ruling, and the six who voted no.
13-17.why_long: At seventeen they can hold two true things: the court's first finding of state genocide, and six judges who voted no. Kuhn says argument is practised, so the script asks whether a split vote is a flaw or just honest judging. Expect 'is Israel next?' South Africa's case against Israel is years off. This ruling is silent on it.

5-7.a: No. It happened far away, to a group their own soldiers turned on. You are safe at home.

8-12.q: What if Myanmar just ignores it?
8-12.a: The world now has a ruling to press Myanmar with. Britain acted the same day.
Trying to destroy a whole group of people for who they are.

13-17.q: Why did it take nine years?
13-17.a: Proving killings is one thing. The court had to prove intent to destroy the group, and that bar is high on purpose.

13-17.q: Does this mean Israel is next?
13-17.a: South Africa's case against Israel is years from a ruling. The judges said nothing about it.
